d4.overview: Domain IV covers the half of the AI lifecycle that begins once a system has been chosen: judging whether and how to deploy it, running the assessments that decision requires, and governing the system while it runs and after it is withdrawn. The BOK scopes it to any deployment context, whether the organization deploys its own proprietary model or a third party's, and it carries the largest question share of the four domains alongside Domain III.
d4.deep_dive:
Domain IV carries **21 to 25 of the 100 scored items**, the joint-largest share with Domain III, and it is the most scenario-heavy part of the exam. Where Domain III governs building a system, Domain IV governs choosing one, adopting it and living with it.

| Competency | What it covers | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **IV.A** Evaluate key factors and risks in the decision to deploy | Context of the use case; AI model types; deployment options including agentic architectures | 6 to 8 |
| **IV.B** Perform key assessment activities | An impact assessment on the selected system; key terms and risks in the vendor or licensing agreement; risks and opportunities of a proprietary model | 5 to 7 |
| **IV.C** Govern deployment and use | Policies, procedures and ethics; continuous monitoring and maintenance; periodic assessments; documentation; secondary use and downstream harm; external communication; deactivation and localization | 9 to 11 |

### The shape of the domain

The three competencies run in sequence in practice. IV.A is a decision: given a business objective, which model type, which environment and which adaptation technique, and does the use case warrant AI at all. IV.B is the diligence that decision triggers: an impact assessment on the system actually chosen, and a hard read of the contract that governs it. IV.C is the long tail: the monitoring, records, audits, incidents, communications and eventual retirement that occupy the rest of the system's working life.

Two facts about the weighting are worth carrying into the exam room. IV.C alone is **9 to 11 questions**, larger than either of the other two competencies and larger than most whole knowledge areas elsewhere in the exam. IV.B is only 5 to 7, but it holds the proprietary-model distinction, which is this domain's most reliable discriminator.

### What "any deployment context" actually changes

The domain description says the obligations apply "whether the company deploys its own proprietary model or a third party's". That is not decoration. It changes who the organization is under the EU AI Act. A firm that places its own model on the market, or that repurposes a third party's general-purpose system into a high-risk use, is a **provider** under Article 25(1)(c), not merely a deployer, and picks up conformity assessment, technical documentation and quality management duties a deployer does not carry. Expect a scenario that hands you an organization and asks which role it occupies.

### What changed in v2.1

Four edits land inside Domain IV:

- **IV.A now names agentic architectures** beside fine-tuning and retrieval augmented generation as a way of deploying a model. This is the only genuinely new technical content in the domain, and it is why agentic AI appears in the blueprint's introduction as something the certification covers.
- **IV.B's "open source agreement" became "licensing agreement"**, which puts proprietary and open-source terms under one heading instead of treating open source as the only contract worth reading.
- **IV.B's proprietary-model item is reframed as risks *and* opportunities.** The older wording read as pure exposure; v2.1 wants the control and capability argument alongside it.
- **The "identify applicable laws" indicators were removed** from III.A and IV.B, and "model" became "system" throughout, matching the BOK's shift from governing a model to governing a system in its deployment context.

### How to hold the domain

Treat Domain IV as a chain of decisions, each with a defensible answer. Does the use case warrant the tool? Which model type and deployment mode fit the objective, the data and the latency requirement? What did the impact assessment find, and what does the contract actually say? Who monitors, what triggers escalation, what gets written down, and how does the system get switched off? Almost every item is one link in that chain, and the distractors are usually answers that sound prudent but belong to a different link.
d4.exam:
Worth 21 to 25 questions and the most scenario-driven domain on the paper. The exam rarely asks you to recall a definition here; it describes a deployment and asks what should happen next, who is accountable, or what the organization has missed. IV.C carries the most items (9 to 11), so do not let the technical appeal of IV.A pull your revision time away from monitoring, records, incidents and retirement.

Three patterns recur. First, a use-case scenario asks you to pick the deployment environment or adaptation technique that fits a stated constraint, where the answer follows from one requirement (latency, data residency, a frequently changing corpus). Second, a vendor scenario asks which contract clause or which role is the problem, and the trap is treating the deployer as if it could outsource its accountability. Third, an incident or retirement scenario asks for the correct order of operations, where the wrong answers are plausible actions taken too early: retraining before preserving evidence, deleting records before the retention period closes, or disclosing before the facts are established.

ch13.overview: IV.A is the decision to deploy. It asks three questions in order: does this use case justify the tool, which kind of model fits it, and where and how should that model run. The competency is small on the paper (6 to 8 questions) but it sets up every assessment and control that follows, because the deployment choice determines the risk surface the rest of Domain IV has to govern.
ch13.deep_dive:
IV.A has three performance indicators, and each is a distinct kind of judgment.

### 1. Context of the use case

The BOK lists business objectives, performance requirements, data availability, ethical considerations and workforce readiness. The first move is the one candidates skip: **deciding whether the use case needs AI at all**. A fixed, repeatable process is usually better served by a deterministic workflow, and adding an autonomous layer where none is required widens the attack surface for no benefit. OWASP calls the principle **least agency**.

The rest of the indicator is readiness. Business objectives come before model capability, because a deployment justified by what a model can do rather than by what the organization needs has no success metric. Data availability decides whether the system is even trainable or groundable. Ethical considerations decide whether the benefit is worth the harm. Workforce readiness decides whether anyone can operate, monitor and override it, and it is the factor most often treated as a training afterthought when it is really a deployment gate.

### 2. AI model types

Four axes get tested: classic versus generative, proprietary versus open source, small versus large, and language versus multimodal. Each has a governance consequence rather than only a performance one. A proprietary model buys capability and support but limits visibility into training data and binds the deployer to terms of service. An open-source model buys transparency and control but moves hosting, security and compliance onto the deployer. Multimodality multiplies the risk surface, since each added modality carries its own failure modes, biases and content risks.

### 3. Deployment options

The environment decision (cloud, on-premises, edge, hybrid) and the adaptation decision (as-is, prompt engineering, fine-tuning, retrieval augmented generation, or an agentic architecture) are separate axes that get confused with each other. The environment is fixed by latency, data residency and outage tolerance. The adaptation technique is fixed by whether the knowledge the model needs changes, and how often. **RAG** answers a corpus that changes often, because retrieval happens at inference and outputs can cite their sources. **Fine-tuning** answers a stable, domain-specific task, at the cost of frozen knowledge and a retraining burden.

v2.1 added **agentic architectures** to this indicator. The governance shift is that an agent acts rather than only producing content, so the controls move from reviewing outputs to bounding actions: what the agent may call, what it may write to, and where a human must approve.

### The connecting thread

All three indicators answer to one question: what does this deployment make possible, and therefore what does it make governable? A use case with a clear objective and available data, on a model whose limitations are known, in an environment whose constraints are understood, is a system IV.B can assess and IV.C can monitor. A deployment that skipped any of those steps arrives at IV.C with risks nobody named.
ch13.exam:
Six to eight questions, and the most technical stretch of the domain. Expect a scenario that states one hard constraint and asks you to pick the deployment environment or adaptation technique: low latency and offline operation points to edge, strict data residency and maximum control point to on-premises, a corpus that changes weekly points to retrieval augmented generation rather than fine-tuning, and a fixed process with no need for judgment points to a deterministic workflow rather than an agent.

The trap is answering the technology question when the stem asks the governance question. "Which deployment mode is most appropriate" is about the stated requirement, not about which is cheapest or most modern. The second trap is treating the model-type axes as independent when a scenario combines them, such as a large multimodal open-source model on edge hardware, where the constraint that actually binds is the one the stem emphasized.

ch11.overview: IV.B is the assessment work that sits between choosing a system and running it. Two indicators: perform or review an impact assessment on the selected system, and identify and evaluate the key terms and risks in the vendor or licensing agreement. A third clause covers the risks and opportunities that come with a proprietary model specifically. It is the smallest competency in the domain (5 to 7 questions) and the one where a wrong answer is most often a category error.
ch11.deep_dive:
IV.B asks what the organization knows before it commits. The impact assessment asks what the system will do to people. The contract review asks what the vendor will and will not stand behind. Together they are the diligence record that IV.C then operates against.

### 1. The impact assessment

The BOK's phrasing is "perform **or review**" an impact assessment on the selected system. The "or review" matters: a deployer that licenses a vendor's model is still responsible for understanding the impacts of the use, and cannot simply adopt the vendor's view. **ISO/IEC 42005:2025** is the method standard for this, published 28 May 2025 as guidance rather than a certifiable requirements standard. It assesses impacts on individuals, groups and society in both directions: benefits and harms, plus failures and foreseeable misuse.

The distinction the exam tests is **42005 versus ISO/IEC 23894**: 42005 asks how the system could affect people and society, 23894 asks what could stop the organization meeting its objectives, and a harm that barely registers as organizational risk can still be a significant impact on the people who bear it.

Two legal overlays matter. Under the GDPR, an Article 35 **DPIA** is mandatory when processing is likely to result in high risk to rights and freedoms. Under the EU AI Act, an Article 27 **fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA)** applies to public bodies and private entities providing public services deploying Annex III systems, and to deployers of the Annex III 5(b) creditworthiness and 5(c) life and health insurance pricing systems. A 42005 record can feed both, but neither law accepts a voluntary standard in place of its own assessment, and 42005 is not harmonised, so it carries no presumption of conformity under Article 40.

### 2. Vendor and licensing terms

This indicator is where Domain IV intersects procurement. The clauses to scrutinize are the ones that move risk onto the deployer: data becoming vendor property, retention for model improvement, onward sharing, outputs not warranted accurate or lawful, and an irrevocable licence over your feedback. Alongside those sit licence family (copyleft terms such as GPL or AGPL can reach your own code), data use restrictions, transparency disclosures, indemnity and liability allocation, and the vendor's security posture.

v2.1 renamed this indicator from "open source agreement" to "licensing agreement": the proprietary contract deserves the same scrutiny, often more, because there is no source code to inspect.

### 3. Proprietary models: risks and opportunities

The third indicator turns on the **proprietary** end of the model-type axis, not on who built the model, and the exam tests which situation the organization is in.

**You built it.** End-to-end ownership means the organization sets the requirements, sources the data, trains the model and answers for everything it does, which under the EU AI Act makes it the **provider**, carrying conformity assessment, technical documentation, logging, quality management and human oversight duties. There is no one else to blame for a biased output.

**You bought it.** A closed third-party model is opaque: you cannot read the training data, often cannot see the version, and may not learn that behaviour changed until users report it. The heightened duties are contractual (audit rights, model-change notice, warranties, data-use limits, exit and portability terms, because contract replaces inspection) and regulatory (the Article 26 deployer duties survive the purchase, and Article 25 makes you the provider if you put your own name on the system, substantially modify it, or change its intended purpose).

The opportunity side is what v2.1 added: ownership buys control over training data, domain fit no vendor serves, trade-secret protection rather than publication, and freedom from a vendor's roadmap, pricing and deprecation. The exam wants both halves recognized, and it wants the role named correctly.
ch11.exam:
Five to seven questions, and the highest-value distinction in the domain is the role question. A scenario describes an organization that licenses a third party's model and then repurposes it for hiring or credit decisions: the answer is usually that it has become a provider under Article 25(1)(c) and now carries provider duties, not that it can rely on the vendor. A scenario that describes a company training its own model and asks who is accountable for a discriminatory output: the answer is the company, because accountability cannot be outsourced.

Know the three assessment instruments and what triggers each. ISO/IEC 42005 is voluntary guidance on impacts to people. A GDPR Article 35 DPIA is a legal duty when processing is likely to be high risk. An EU AI Act Article 27 FRIA is a legal duty for in-scope deployers of Annex III systems. Confusing which one is mandatory, and for whom, is the most common way to lose an IV.B item. The other reliable trap is a contract question where the wrong answer assumes the vendor's warranty covers the deployer's liability.

ch12.overview: IV.C is the largest competency in the domain and the largest single block of governance content on the exam: 9 to 11 questions on what happens once a system is live. It runs from policies and monitoring through audits, incident handling, business records and external communication, and closes with the policy and controls to deactivate or localize a system. Everything here is a repeated, documented practice rather than a one-time decision.
ch12.deep_dive:
IV.C has seven performance indicators, and they form a cycle rather than a list: you operate the system, you watch it, you assess it, you write it down, you communicate, and eventually you switch it off.

### 1. Policies, procedures, best practices and ethics

The BOK names data governance, risk management, issue management and user training. The practical test of a deployment policy is whether it is **traceable, repeatable and reversible**: version control over models and configuration, mandatory separation between development, staging and production, and a rollback procedure in every deployment plan. User training belongs here rather than in HR, because a user who cannot tell when to distrust the model is an unmanaged control.

### 2. Continuous monitoring and maintenance

AI systems degrade because the world moves, not because the code rots. Monitoring covers prediction quality, input data, latency, resource use, fairness across subgroups, and drift. Three drift types get tested: **data (covariate) drift** is the input distribution shifting, **label drift** is the outcome distribution shifting, and **concept drift** is the relationship between inputs and outputs changing, so the same input now implies a different outcome. Maintenance is the scheduled response: periodic evaluation, retraining at a cadence set by volatility and risk, dependency and compliance updates, and hotfixes for urgent failures. Retraining is a tradeoff, not a default, because fresher data can also destabilise a model.

### 3. Periodic assessments

The BOK lists audits, red teaming, threat modeling and security testing. These are the deliberate, scheduled counterpart to continuous monitoring, and they test the policies and processes as well as the model.

### 4. Documentation

Incidents, issues, risks and post-market monitoring plans all get written down. The exam's emphasis is on post-market monitoring being a **documented, forward-looking plan established before release**: what real-world data is collected, how it is reviewed, by whom, and what threshold triggers action. A dashboard is one input to that plan, not a substitute for it. Metrics without thresholds and a defined escalation path produce reports nobody acts on.

### 5. Secondary and unintended use, and downstream harm

Approval attaches to a use case in context, not to a model in the abstract. Repurposing an approved model for a different decision, population or consequence requires a fresh impact assessment, risk review and approval; updating the model card documents the change but does not authorise it. Downstream harms are the consequences felt by people and systems nobody considered at design time, and forecasting them means extending the review beyond direct users to second- and third-order effects.

### 6. External communication plans

Capabilities and limitations, incident notifications, regulatory reporting and user-facing transparency. The recurring trap is overclaiming: overstating what a system can do invites regulatory scrutiny and litigation, and the disclosure obligations that bite are specific (Article 50 transparency, Article 73 serious incident reporting, GDPR Article 34 breach notification to data subjects).

### 7. Deactivation and localization

A policy and controls to take a system offline, or restrict it to a region, on regulatory or performance grounds. For high-risk systems under the EU AI Act, Article 14(4)(e) requires a stop function that halts the system in a safe state, and Article 26(5) requires deployers to suspend use and inform the provider and authority when a risk emerges. Localization is the regional variant, driven by data sovereignty, ethical norms or a legal prohibition, and delivered through separate model instances, federated learning or a modular architecture.
ch12.exam:
Nine to eleven questions, the heaviest block in the domain, and almost entirely scenario-based. The stem usually describes something that has gone wrong or is about to, and the answer is the correct next action: preserve evidence before retraining, assess the breach against statutory clocks before announcing the technical fix, escalate by severity, or trigger the documented threshold rather than improvising.

Learn the drift vocabulary cold, because it is cheap points. If the stem says input quality is unchanged but the model's behaviour has shifted, that is concept drift. If the inputs have changed, that is data or covariate drift. If the distribution of outcomes has moved, that is label drift. The second reliable pattern is the difference between an incident and an issue, and the third is the difference between documenting a change and authorising one. A model card update records that a model is being used for something new; it does not approve the new use.

t_deployfactors.overview: The context of the use case is IV.A's first indicator, and it is the one candidates treat as throat-clearing. It is not: the five factors the BOK names decide whether the deployment has a defensible purpose, a success metric, the data to work with, an ethical case, and people able to run it. Get this wrong and every later control is protecting the wrong thing.
t_deployfactors.deep_dive:
The BOK lists five factors: **business objectives, performance requirements, data availability, ethical considerations and workforce readiness**. They run in order, and each one can stop the deployment.

### Business objectives first, capability second

The single most common failure in a deployment decision is starting from what a model can do. A deployment justified by capability has no success metric, so nobody can later say whether it worked or whether it caused harm. The governance move is to state the objective in the organization's terms (reduce claims processing time, widen credit access) and then ask what performance level would count as meeting it. That statement becomes the threshold that post-market monitoring measures against in IV.C.

### Does the use case need AI at all

Before the five factors, there is a question the BOK leaves implicit and OWASP names explicitly: **least agency**. Where the process is fixed and repeatable, a deterministic workflow is cheaper, testable, explainable and far harder to attack than an autonomous system. Deploying autonomy where it adds nothing widens the attack surface without buying capability. Expect a scenario where the correct answer is that the process should not be agentic, or not AI-driven, at all.

### Data availability and suitability

Availability is not the same as suitability. The questions are whether the data exists at the volume and quality the task needs, whether the organization has the legal entitlement to use it for training or inference, and whether the data is representative of the population the system will affect. Internal data is not automatically safe data: repurposing records collected for one purpose to train a model can breach purpose limitation and data minimisation, and the lawful basis for AI training has to be documented rather than assumed.

### Ethical considerations

This is where the deployment is weighed rather than measured. The relevant questions are who benefits, who bears the harm, whether the harm falls on people who cannot refuse, and whether the use is one the organization would defend publicly. Some of this is settled by law (a prohibited practice under EU AI Act Article 5, or a use that triggers a DPIA under GDPR Article 35), but most of it is a judgment the organization has to make and record, which is why ISO/IEC 42005 treats impacts as two-sided: benefits as well as harms.

### Workforce readiness

Workforce readiness is a deployment gate, not a training task. It covers whether the intended users have the skills to operate the system, whether they can tell when to distrust it, whether administrators can manage and monitor it, and whether the organization retains enough of the underlying skill to keep operating if the system is unavailable. The last point is easy to overlook and it is what makes a kill switch meaningful: a fallback nobody can execute is not a fallback.

### The connecting thread

These five factors are the inputs to every later decision in the domain. They set the success metric that IV.C monitors, the risk appetite that IV.B assesses against, and the oversight capability that the deactivation policy in IV.C depends on. A deployment that skipped them does not fail at go-live; it fails months later, when nobody can say what the system was supposed to achieve or who was watching it.
t_deployfactors.exam:
Expect a scenario that describes an organization adopting AI and asks what it should establish first. The answer is usually the business objective and success metric, not the model selection and not the training programme. A second pattern gives you a deployment that has already gone wrong and asks what was missing: no defined threshold, no representative data, or no user able to recognize a bad output.

The trap is the answer that sounds most responsible in isolation. A scenario about a company deploying AI for hiring will offer "run a bias audit" and "define what success looks like". Both are good practice, but if the stem says the objective was never articulated, the audit has nothing to measure against. Read which factor the stem left out.

t_modeltypes.overview: Model type is IV.A's second indicator, and the exam tests it as a set of four trade-offs rather than four definitions: classic versus generative, proprietary versus open source, small versus large, and language versus multimodal. Each axis changes what the organization can see, what it owes and who it can hold responsible, which is why the choice belongs in a deployment evaluation rather than in an engineering stand-up.
t_modeltypes.deep_dive:
### Classic versus generative

Classic AI (rule-based systems, statistical models, decision trees, classifiers) produces a bounded output against a defined target: a label, a score, a recommendation. Generative models produce open-ended content. The governance difference is that a classifier's failure is a wrong answer with a measurable error rate, while a generative model's failure can be fluent, plausible and wrong, and its output can be reused as input somewhere else. Generative systems add their own failure families: confabulation, synthetic media abuse, and the privacy exposure that comes from training on unfiltered web data.

### Proprietary versus open source

This is the axis with the largest legal consequence. A **proprietary model** gives the deployer vendor support, a managed service and often the strongest capability, at the cost of limited visibility into training data and model behaviour, binding terms of service, and dependence on the vendor for updates, incident support and continuity. An **open-source model** gives transparency, inspection, local control and the freedom to fine-tune, at the cost of moving hosting, security, patching and compliance onto the deployer. Neither is safer by default.

The trap is assuming open source means unencumbered. Open weights are still licensed, and the licence governs commercial use, attribution and, for copyleft terms such as GPL or AGPL, what happens to code that incorporates the model. Licence review belongs in the deployment decision, not after it, and v2.1 renamed IV.B's indicator from "open source agreement" to "licensing agreement" precisely because the proprietary contract deserves the same reading.

### Small versus large

The trade-off runs in both directions. Larger models generally offer broader capability and better performance on complex tasks, but cost more per call, respond more slowly, and present a wider surface for attack and misuse. Smaller models are cheaper, faster and easier to constrain, but may underperform on the hard cases. The governing question is fitness for the specific use case, not maximum capability, and the exam's wrong answers are usually the ones that treat more capability as strictly better. Quantization and distillation exist to move a model down this axis without a full retrain.

### Language versus multimodal

A language model handles text; a multimodal model handles combinations of text, image, audio and video. Multimodality expands the use cases and expands the risk surface in step. Each added modality brings its own failure modes (image models misread faces and scenes, audio models transcribe accents unevenly), its own bias profile, and its own content risks, including the ability to generate convincing synthetic media. A deployment that justifies multimodality by capability alone has not done the assessment.

### How the axes combine

Real scenarios combine all four, and the constraint that binds is the one the stem emphasizes. A large multimodal open-source model on edge hardware is constrained by the hardware, not by the licence. A small proprietary model in a regulated data flow is constrained by residency and terms, not by capability. Read which axis the scenario is actually testing before choosing.
t_modeltypes.exam:
The exam asks you to pick the model type that fits a stated constraint, and the constraint is always in the stem. Frequently changing knowledge points to retrieval rather than a bigger model. Tight data residency or a need to inspect the weights points to open source. Low latency or an offline requirement points to a small model or edge inference. A need for vendor indemnification points to proprietary, with the licence and liability terms read carefully.

The most common wrong answer treats open source as inherently safer or inherently cheaper. Open source shifts cost and responsibility to the deployer rather than removing either, and the licence still binds. The second trap is a multimodal scenario where the question is about the added risk surface, not the added capability.

t_deployopts.overview: Deployment options are two decisions that get collapsed into one. The first is the environment: cloud, on-premises, edge or hybrid. The second is the adaptation technique: use the model as-is, steer it with prompts, fine-tune it, ground it with retrieval, or wrap it in an agentic architecture. The environment follows from latency, residency and outage tolerance. The technique follows from whether the knowledge the model needs changes, and how often.
t_deployopts.deep_dive:
### The environment decision

| Mode | What it buys | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Cloud** | Scale, elasticity, managed infrastructure, fast integration | Less control over data locality; third-party and transfer questions |
| **On-premises** | Maximum control, data residency, strict compliance fit | Capital cost, lower elasticity, operational burden |
| **Edge** | Low latency, works offline, data never leaves the device | Limited compute, model size constraints, harder update and monitoring logistics |
| **Hybrid** | Splits the difference, such as edge or on-prem inference with cloud training | Added architectural complexity and integration overhead |

The exam's tell is the requirement, not the technology. "Low latency plus outage tolerance plus sensitive data on site" is edge. "Strict data residency plus maximum control" is on-premises. "Elastic demand and a small team" is cloud. Hybrid is the answer only when the stem describes a genuine split, and the right follow-up is to check where inference actually happens. Deployment mode should be settled in the design phase, because containerization and orchestration choices follow from it.

### The adaptation ladder

**As-is (with prompt engineering).** No weights change. Prompt engineering shapes the instructions, context and examples sent to a generative model, including system prompts and few-shot examples. It is the cheapest way to improve output and the least durable, because it is not enforced by anything: a prompt-layer limit can be bypassed or simply forgotten, which is why the exam prefers a control enforced at the tool or system layer wherever the risk is real.

**Fine-tuning.** Additional training on targeted data adapts the model's weights to a domain or task. It buys consistent behaviour and domain fit, and it costs a retraining pipeline, a maintenance burden, and knowledge frozen at training time. It changes the model, which means it triggers change management, a fresh evaluation, and in regulated contexts a reassessment.

**Retrieval augmented generation (RAG).** The model retrieves relevant external content at query time and conditions its answer on it. Updates to the corpus take effect immediately with no retraining, and the output can cite its sources, which is why RAG is the answer for a corpus that changes often and the reason it reduces confabulation in enterprise settings. The trade-off is that the retrieval layer is now part of the attack surface: a poisoned document is a poisoned answer.

**Agentic architectures.** v2.1 added these to the indicator. Instead of producing content for a person to use, an agent plans and acts over several steps through tools. The governance shift is from reviewing outputs to bounding actions, and the controls move to least-privilege permissions, approval checkpoints and kill switches. The first question is still whether the use case needs an agent at all.

**From scratch.** Training a model from nothing is rarely proportionate, and the exam treats it as the distractor unless the stem describes a capability nobody offers and the organization has the data and the resources to build it.

### Efficiency techniques

**Quantization** reduces numerical precision (32-bit to 8-bit) to shrink the model and cut inference latency. **Distillation** trains a smaller student model to approximate a larger teacher. Both trade a little accuracy for size and speed, and both are legitimate ways to meet a latency or edge constraint without changing the deployment story.
t_deployopts.exam:
This is where the scenario items concentrate in IV.A. The pattern is a stated constraint and a request for the right option: a frequently changing corpus points to retrieval augmented generation rather than fine-tuning; a stable domain task with consistent formatting points to fine-tuning; a latency ceiling or an offline requirement points to edge or a smaller quantized model; a need to keep data inside a jurisdiction points to on-premises or a regional instance.

The most reliable trap is fine-tuning offered as the answer for a knowledge problem. Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves, not what it knows about a corpus that keeps moving, and it freezes knowledge at training time. The second trap is a prompt-layer control offered where the risk is serious: telling a model not to do something is not the same as removing its ability to do it.

t_agentic.overview: Agentic AI is the one genuinely new technical subject in BOK v2.1. A generative assistant produces content that a person then uses; an agent plans, decides and acts through tools, with some independence from human direction. Governance therefore shifts from reviewing outputs to bounding actions, and the controls that matter become least-privilege permissions, approval checkpoints, monitoring and a kill switch.
t_agentic.deep_dive:
### What makes an agent different

In the IMDA framework an agent has some independence in planning, deciding and acting over several steps to reach a goal a user sets. Today's enterprise agents usually pair a language model with instructions, memory, tools and controls, and an **agentic AI system** is one or more such agents working alone or together.

| | Generative assistant | AI agent |
|---|---|---|
| Main output | Content for a human to use | Actions in other systems, plus content |
| Steps | Usually one prompt, one response | A multi-step plan, executed and revised |
| Reach | The conversation | Tools, APIs, computers and browsers, other agents |
| Typical failure | Wrong or harmful content | Wrong, unauthorised or irreversible actions |

### Two dials

Risk scales along two independent dials. **Action space** is what the agent can do, fixed by the tools it may call and the permissions on them: sandbox only, internal systems or external systems; read or write. **Autonomy** is how freely it decides what to do, set by its instructions and the level of human involvement. An agent that reads a database and drafts a summary and one that writes to that database and emails the result have very different risk profiles, and the difference is the permissions, not the model.

IMDA describes four levels of human involvement, from the agent proposing and a human operating (approve every step) through collaboration and exception-based approval, to the agent operating while a human observes.

### How risk scales

Agents inherit ordinary software flaws and model risks, and add pathways through **planning** (a plan that misreads intent or drifts), **tools** (the wrong tool, the wrong input, or a tool turned into an exfiltration route by injected instructions) and **protocols** (a malicious MCP server carrying code that leaks data). IMDA names five harm kinds: erroneous actions, unauthorised actions, biased or unfair actions, data breaches, and disruption to connected systems. Multi-agent systems add interaction risk on top: cascading failures compound one mistake across later steps, shared context leaks data to less secure agents, and agents can miscoordinate, conflict or collude. Emergent behaviour is the hardest case, because testing each agent alone cannot predict it.

### The controls that carry the weight

- **Least privilege, capped by the authorising human.** Scoped, time- or session-bound, non-transferable, with explicit escalation for more, and never beyond what the authorising human may do.
- **Deterministic beats prompt-based.** Block a tool with an access control instead of asking the model not to use it.
- **Human approval checkpoints** for high-stakes, irreversible, atypical or user-defined actions, enforced at the system level and audited for rubber-stamping.
- **Unique agent identity**, verifiable, tied to a supervising agent, human or department, and centrally catalogued to curb sprawl.
- **Kill switches and credential revocation**, with a manual fallback and preserved, tamper-proof logs.
- **Fail-safe by default.** When the approval service is down, deny the action. A time-out that lets the agent proceed is fail-open.

### How the law attaches

No separate agent category exists. Article 3(1) of the EU AI Act defines an AI system as one designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy whose outputs can influence physical or virtual environments, and agents fit squarely. The risk tier follows the **use**, not the architecture: an agent that screens job applications falls under Annex III point 4(a), one that scores creditworthiness under 5(b). A deployer that repurposes a general-purpose system into a high-risk use becomes its provider under Article 25(1)(c). Under the GDPR an agent that decides is an automated decision, and Recital 71's examples (automatic refusal of a credit application, e-recruiting without human intervention) describe what an autonomous agent does.
t_agentic.exam:
Agentic AI is new content, so expect it to be tested directly: which risk is this, which control answers it, and does the use case need an agent at all. The OWASP classification rules are worth memorizing, because the codes are the cleanest discriminator. Misusing privileges the agent already holds is ASI02 (tool misuse); gaining privileges it should not have is ASI03; misuse ending in code execution is ASI05. Persistent corruption of stored context is ASI06 (memory poisoning); a one-off malicious prompt stays under the LLM Top 10's prompt injection entry. ASI01 is goal hijack, typically via indirect prompt injection hidden in content the agent reads. ASI08 is propagation, used when a defect fans out across agents; classify the originating defect under its own entry. ASI09 is human over-reliance; ASI10 is the agent itself drifting.

The second reliable pattern is the two dials. A question that changes the agent's tools or permissions is changing its action space; a question that changes its instructions or the number of approval steps is changing its autonomy. The third is that accountability stays with the deployer: an answer that shifts responsibility to the agent vendor is wrong, and the fix for vendor opacity is disclosures, tested controls, a narrower scope or a different supplier.

t_deployimpact.overview: The deployment impact assessment is the diligence IV.B requires before a system goes live. It asks how the system, and the ways it could foreseeably be used, will affect individuals, groups and society. ISO/IEC 42005:2025 is the method standard, and the exam tests it against two neighbouring instruments: the GDPR DPIA and the EU AI Act FRIA. Knowing which is voluntary, which is mandatory and who must perform each is worth real points.
t_deployimpact.deep_dive:
### What ISO/IEC 42005 is

ISO/IEC 42005:2025 was published on 28 May 2025 and is **guidance, not a requirements standard**. Nobody can be certified to 42005; the certifiable standard in the family is ISO/IEC 42001, which *requires* an AI system impact assessment (clauses 6.1.4 and 8.4, Annex A objective A.5) and says little about how to perform one. 42005 fills that gap.

Two ideas carry most of the questions. Its **lens is people, not the organization**: it assesses impacts on individuals, groups of individuals and societies that the system or its foreseeable applications can affect. And it runs **across the lifecycle**, starting at design, gating deployment, and repeating whenever the system, its use or its context changes.

### The distinction from ISO/IEC 23894

This is the cleanest discriminator in the topic. **42005** asks how this system could affect people and society, for better or worse. **23894** asks what could stop the organization meeting its objectives, extending ISO 31000 with AI-specific guidance. A harm that barely registers as organizational risk can still be a significant impact on the people who bear it. 42005's Annex B shows how impact findings feed the 23894 risk process, so they are complements, not alternatives. Exam tell: "harm to the people affected" points to 42005; "risk to the business" points to 23894.

### What an assessment records

Clause 5 sets up the organization's **process**: timing, scope, responsibilities, thresholds for sensitive and restricted uses, and the perform, analyse, record, approve and review cycle. Clause 6 defines what **one assessment** records: scope; AI system information including purpose, intended uses and unintended uses; data information and quality; algorithm and model information; the deployment environment; relevant interested parties; actual and reasonably foreseeable impacts, meaning benefits and harms, failures and foreseeable misuse; and the measures that address the harms and secure the benefits. An assessment that lists only harms is incomplete, and so is one with no unintended uses, because the standard asks about both what the organization plans and what could occur anyway.

### Timing and reassessment

Assess at design, before deployment as a gate, during operation through monitoring and periodic review, and on significant change. The reassessment triggers are a change of intended use or purpose, a significant change to the system such as new data types or retraining, a change in the legal or policy environment, and monitoring or feedback revealing something the assessment did not anticipate. A demand-forecasting model that starts rating individual workers is the textbook trigger.

### Against the DPIA and the FRIA

| | ISO/IEC 42005 | GDPR Article 35 DPIA | EU AI Act Article 27 FRIA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nature | Voluntary guidance | Legal duty when triggered | Legal duty for in-scope deployers |
| Who | Any organization developing, providing or using AI | The controller | Public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) and 5(c) systems |
| Trigger | The organization's own lifecycle points and thresholds | Processing likely to result in high risk to rights and freedoms | Before first use of an Annex III high-risk system (point 2, critical infrastructure, excluded) |
| Focus | Benefits and harms to individuals, groups and society | Risks to data subjects from processing personal data | Impact on the fundamental rights of affected people |

Three points follow. A deployer cannot rely on its vendor's assessment, because 42005 applies to organizations that develop, **provide or use** AI. One well-built 42005 record can feed both the DPIA and the FRIA, and Article 27(4) lets a FRIA build on an existing DPIA rather than repeat it. But neither law accepts a voluntary standard in place of its own assessment, and 42005 is not a harmonised standard, so it carries no presumption of conformity under Article 40.
t_deployimpact.exam:
The exam's favourite question here is which instrument applies and who owes it. Three facts settle most items: 42005 is guidance and cannot be certified; a GDPR Article 35 DPIA is mandatory when processing is likely to be high risk; an EU AI Act Article 27 FRIA applies to public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) creditworthiness and 5(c) life and health insurance pricing systems.

The trap is treating 42005 as a substitute. It never replaces a DPIA or a FRIA, and it gives no presumption of conformity. The second trap is a deployer arguing it can adopt its vendor's impact assessment; the standard is explicit that organizations which merely *use* AI are in scope. The third is an assessment presented as a one-off before launch: reassessment on significant change is part of the method.

t_vendorterms.overview: Vendor and licensing terms are where Domain IV meets procurement, and the exam treats them as a risk-reading exercise rather than a legal one. The question is always which clause moves risk onto the deployer, and what the organization is left holding. Two extra layers matter: a copyleft licence can reach the deployer's own code, and deploying a proprietary model generally makes the organization the provider under the EU AI Act.
t_vendorterms.deep_dive:
### What to look for in the agreement

A vendor agreement for AI should pin down data usage rights, performance guarantees, liability allocation, audit rights and compliance obligations. The clauses that matter most are the ones that transfer risk quietly:

| Red flag | What the deployer loses |
|---|---|
| Data sent to the model becomes vendor property | Ownership of its own data |
| Data may be retained for model improvement | Confidentiality; a purpose-limitation problem |
| Data may be passed to third parties | Control over onward sharing and transfers |
| Outputs are not warranted accurate or lawful | Any vendor accountability for the thing you deploy |
| An irrevocable licence over your feedback | Intellectual property in your own improvements |

Alongside those sit the terms that decide whether the deployer can ever check the vendor's claims: disclosure of training data sources and model lineage, performance evaluation evidence, audit mechanisms, security certifications (ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 42001, SOC 2 Type II), incident notification timelines, and whether the vendor carries cyber liability insurance. Opacity is the core problem with a vendor-hosted model: if the vendor will not disclose capabilities and data handling, and will not offer scoped API keys, per-agent identity tokens or logging of tool calls, the options are a narrower use case, a different supplier, or an in-house build.

### Licensing families

Open weights are still licensed, and the licence family decides what the deployer may do:

- **Permissive** terms (MIT, Apache 2.0) impose little beyond attribution and notice retention.
- **Copyleft** terms (GPL, AGPL) can require that code incorporating the model be disclosed under the same licence, which is a real exposure for a for-profit product that embeds a model in its own codebase.
- **Source-available and non-commercial** terms restrict commercial use outright. Integrating a non-commercial model into a commercial product is the textbook IP infringement scenario.

Licence review belongs before the deployment decision, not after it, and it applies to every component in the chain, including fine-tuned derivatives and any third-party tools an agent calls.

### Proprietary model obligations

Deploying a third party's proprietary model does not make the deployer passive. The heightened duties are increased contractual obligations, reliance on vendor claims that cannot be independently verified, potential for higher liability exposure, and dependence on the vendor for updates, incident support and continuity. If the vendor deprecates the model or the API, the deployer inherits a retirement project it did not plan.

The sharper point is legal. Under the EU AI Act, an organization that puts its own model on the market is a **provider**, and an organization that repurposes a third party's system (including a general-purpose AI system) into a high-risk use is treated as its provider under **Article 25(1)(c)**. Provider duties (conformity assessment, technical documentation, logging, quality management, human oversight, incident reporting) cannot be delegated to a vendor. **Accountability cannot be outsourced**: the organization vetted and selected the third party, and it chose the use.

### The opportunities side

v2.1 reframed this indicator as risks *and* opportunities. The upside of building rather than buying is control over training data and quality, the ability to tune the model to a domain no vendor serves, protection through trade secret rather than publication, freedom from a vendor's roadmap, pricing and deprecation, and the ability to answer a regulator's questions about the model directly rather than through a supplier.
t_vendorterms.exam:
Expect a contract scenario where you identify the clause that should have been negotiated, or a role scenario where you identify who carries the obligation. The recurring trap is an answer that assumes the vendor's warranty covers the deployer's liability; outputs are frequently expressly unwarranted, and even where they are warranted, the deployer's statutory duties under the AI Act are its own.

The second trap is a licence question where "open source" is treated as "no restrictions". Copyleft and non-commercial terms both bite. The third is the provider shift: a scenario where a company fine-tunes or repurposes someone else's general-purpose model into hiring, credit or another Annex III use, and the correct answer is that it now carries provider duties under Article 25(1)(c).

t_riskmgmt.overview: Risk management and forecasting is the analytical spine of IV.C. AI risk is an overlay on enterprise risk management rather than a separate discipline, but it brings failure modes traditional IT risk does not: probabilistic outputs, models that change with retraining, third-party model dependencies, and harms felt at societal scale. Forecasting is what turns monitoring data into a decision about what to change next.
t_riskmgmt.deep_dive:
### Why AI risk is not ordinary IT risk

Conventional IT risk frameworks cover availability, data loss and system failure. AI risk adds four things: **probabilistic behaviour**, where an output is a distribution rather than a correct answer; **evolving outputs**, because retraining, feedback loops and environmental inputs change the model; **third-party model dependencies**, since most organizations consume someone else's model, open-source weights or a cloud service; and **societal-level impacts**, including discrimination, misinformation and environmental cost. One framing worth remembering: AI risks sit at or above Layer 7 of the OSI model, because they are socio-technical risks about data and decisions, not infrastructure logic.

A second principle carries the domain: **a system secure today may not remain secure tomorrow**. AI risk management has to be proactive rather than periodic, because the model and its environment both move.

### The definition of risk, and the matrix

**Risk** is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, where the deviation can be positive, negative or both, characterized by drivers, potential events, consequences and likelihood. ISO/IEC 23894 takes its structure from ISO 31000 and adds AI-specific guidance to each of the eight principles, of which **dynamic** matters most for AI, because systems that learn change their own risk profile.

A **probability-severity matrix** plots likelihood against impact to prioritize treatment. It ranks and prioritizes risks; it does not measure them. The NIST AI RMF equivalent is MANAGE 1.2, treatment prioritized by impact, likelihood and available resources.

### The register

AI risks belong in the enterprise risk register, with fields for the system or application, the risk description, associated use cases, likelihood and impact scores, the treatment decision and its decision-maker, the mitigation strategy, the residual risk after mitigation, the risk owner, and a review schedule. Two properties matter for AI specifically. The register is **dynamic**, because retraining and drift change the entries. And it is **bidirectionally linked to incidents**: when an incident reveals a risk nobody had considered, that risk gets added; every incident should also trace to the risks already on the register when it occurred.

### Forecasting techniques

Forecasting asks how the system behaves under pressure rather than how it behaved in test. **Drift detection** watches the three drift types (data or covariate drift shifts the input distribution, concept drift changes the relationship between inputs and outputs, label drift shifts the outcome distribution), with statistical tests triggering retraining or alerts at thresholds. **Feedback loop anticipation**: recommendation engines and predictive policing change the environment, the changed environment becomes training data, and the model amplifies its own bias. **Simulation** uses digital twins, synthetic data and simulated environments to test adversarial and edge-case behaviour before production sees it. **Threat modelling** supplies the attack paths, with MITRE ATLAS as the AI-specific knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques, modelled on ATT&CK, and kill chain analysis, attack trees, TARA and PASTA as related methodologies.

### Secondary use and downstream harm

The hardest part of forecasting is anticipating use the organization never intended. **Secondary use** is AI output applied to a purpose different from the original intent: content reused as training data elsewhere, outputs chained into another system, or a benign tool repurposed for harm (an image upscaler turned into a deepfake generator). **Downstream harm** is the consequence felt by people and systems nobody considered. The answer is to extend risk review beyond direct users to second- and third-order effects, using stakeholder impact mapping, recursive scenario modelling, external consultation and misuse testing.
t_riskmgmt.exam:
Most items here are vocabulary and classification. Know that risk includes positive deviation, that the probability-severity matrix ranks rather than measures, that MITRE ATLAS is the AI-specific adversary knowledge base and STRIDE is a threat-modelling framework, and that NIST AI RMF's MANAGE function is where treatment, monitoring and decommissioning live.

The scenario trap is treating a periodic audit as sufficient risk management. The domain's principle is that AI risk is dynamic, so the right answer is usually continuous monitoring plus a threshold that triggers action, not an annual review. The second trap is an answer that stops at direct users when the stem describes harm to people who never touched the system; secondary use and downstream harm are the point of the indicator.

t_audit.overview: Audits and assurance are the deliberate, scheduled half of IV.C: the periodic checks that a system still does what it claims, that the policies around it are being followed, and that the evidence exists to prove both. The exam distinguishes assurance (the overall program that builds justified confidence) from an audit or a red-team test (a technique inside it), and it expects you to know which technique answers which question.
t_audit.deep_dive:
### Assurance is the program; an audit is one technique

**AI assurance** is the combined work of checking, and showing to others, whether an AI system deserves trust: impact assessments, bias and compliance audits, conformity assessment, performance testing, formal verification and certification. An audit or a red-team test is one assurance technique. The distinction matters because the exam offers audit as a synonym for assurance, and the correct answer is that assurance is the overall program that produces justified confidence for regulators, customers and the board.

An **audit** itself is a systematic, independent examination of a system's design, data, outputs and governance against established criteria. It can be first party (internal), second party (a customer or partner auditing a supplier) or third party (an independent external auditor). Under the EU AI Act, conformity assessment for high-risk systems is carried out against the Chapter III requirements and, for certain systems, by a **notified body**, which is what makes "internal audit staff can sign this off" the wrong answer in a regulated scenario.

### The techniques, and what each answers

| Technique | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Performance audit** | Does the system meet its stated criteria across accuracy, fairness, robustness, performance and generalization? |
| **Model validation** | Do the development claims hold up, and does behaviour match between test and production? |
| **Red teaming** | How does the system behave under adversarial and misuse conditions? |
| **Threat modelling** | What are the attack paths against this specific system? |
| **Security testing** | Can confidentiality and integrity be broken? |
| **Compliance audit** | Are the applicable laws, policies and contractual terms actually followed? |

Performance criteria are set in the design phase (business alignment, context sensitivity, stakeholder expectations, fairness, precision, robustness) and audits test against them. Models often behave differently in production than in controlled test environments, so when a production system fails a criterion, the follow-up is to reproduce it in test and find the difference.

**Red teaming** is structured adversarial simulation: prompt injection and jailbreak testing, evasion attacks, poisoning, functionality misuse, social engineering. It should cover the wider ecosystem (infrastructure, APIs, integration layers, data pipelines) rather than model parameters alone, and it targets personnel as well as the system. **Threat modelling** extends traditional methods to AI-specific attack surfaces: STRIDE adapted for AI maps spoofing and tampering onto prompt injection and data poisoning, information disclosure onto model theft, and elevation of privilege onto unauthorised API chaining. MITRE ATLAS is the AI-specific knowledge base, with kill chain analysis, attack trees, TARA and PASTA as related methodologies, and **threat hunting** is the proactive complement: searching for indicators of compromise rather than waiting for an alert. **Security testing** for AI adds model extraction, inference attacks, membership inference, re-identification testing and adversarial robustness testing.

### Documentation and reporting

The assurance program is only as good as its evidence. Audit documentation includes the audit charter, findings and recommendations, red-teaming logs and the scenarios tested, threat models with attack paths and mitigations, reproducible test sets, model version histories and deployment metadata, and evidence of remediation. Records should be **immutable and timestamped**, held to a retention schedule, access-controlled and encrypted, with legal counsel consulted on retention periods. The preparation list is short: one source of truth for documentation, immutable logs, internal dry runs, a named owner per compliance area, and coaching for the people who will sit in front of the auditor.
t_audit.exam:
The reliable distinctions are assurance versus audit, first versus third party, and which technique fits the stem. If a scenario asks whether a system deserves trust and how to show that to a regulator, the answer is assurance. If it asks for an independent examination against criteria, that is an audit. If it asks how the system behaves under deliberate attack, that is red teaming. If it asks what could be attacked and how, that is threat modelling.

Two traps recur. First, a question offers "internal audit" for a system where the EU AI Act requires conformity assessment by a notified body; the internal option is wrong. Second, a question asks how to find problems before they surface, and the wrong answer is waiting for monitoring to alert: threat hunting is the proactive answer. Also remember that audits test the policies and processes, not only the model, and that continuous monitoring detects degradation earlier than a periodic audit will.

t_incident.overview: Incident management is where IV.C becomes operational. The exam tests three things: the difference between an incident and an issue, the order of response steps, and who must be told what, by when. The domain's recurring warning is that the technically obvious first move (retrain the model) is usually the wrong one, because it destroys the evidence the investigation and the regulator both need.
t_incident.deep_dive:
### Incident versus issue

An **incident** is unexpected behaviour involving an AI system that causes, or has the potential to cause, harm, operational disruption or regulatory concern: a recommendation system surfacing illegal content, a chatbot giving incorrect medical advice, or unexpected degradation from drift. An **issue** is undesirable behaviour, a complaint or a shortcoming that does not rise to that severity but still needs formal tracking: minor inconsistencies, sporadic misclassification, tester feedback.

The boundary is **severity plus context**, not the type of event. A poorly ranked search result is an annoyance; a misclassification in a diagnostic tool can be life-threatening.

### The response lifecycle

**Detection, triage, communication, investigation, containment, eradication, recovery, after-action review, documentation.** A shorter mnemonic that fits the exam's ordering questions: **contain, assess, investigate, remediate, notify, learn**. Two ordering rules matter more than the list itself. Preserve evidence before retraining, because retraining destroys the state you need to explain what happened. And never disable logging during an incident, because that destroys the audit trail you are legally required to keep.

Severity classification drives escalation: critical (widespread harm, regulatory violation or systemic failure), major (significant user impact or breakdown of a core function), moderate (isolated, limited exposure), minor (no external impact, handled internally). Note that not every incident is a bug: some come from **misaligned objectives**, where a model trained to maximize engagement promotes polarizing content without ever malfunctioning, so the fix may be a change of objective rather than a change of code.

### Root cause and the culture question

Root causes are usually one of: model brittleness, insufficient robustness, poor or unrepresentative training data, misaligned objectives, over-reliance on automation with absent oversight, inadequate testing, model or data drift, or prompt-design failures in generative systems. Understanding them takes a multidisciplinary review. The stated goal is to learn and improve, not to assign blame, because psychological safety is what makes people report the near misses that precede real incidents.

### Monitoring as the detection layer

Incident management depends on operation and monitoring feeding it. Monitoring covers prediction quality, input data, latency, resource use, fairness across subgroups and drift, with alerting on thresholds. Leading indicators of systemic risk (a spike in edge-case failures, repeated human overrides, declining trust, rising toxicity, growth in misuse cases) act as **tripwires** that trigger review or suspension, and any of them is treated as an incident. **Resilience** is the other side: the ability to recover the operational state quickly after an incident.

### Public disclosure

Disclosure triggers vary by law and context, and include deployment of a high-risk system, material performance degradation, safety failure, a significant breach affecting AI inputs or outputs, misleading output affecting health or safety, and behaviour outside the intended use case. The obligations that actually bite are specific: **EU AI Act Article 73** requires providers of high-risk systems to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority, generally within 15 days of becoming aware (10 days for a death, and sooner for widespread infringement or serious and irreversible disruption); **GDPR Articles 33 and 34** run their own 72-hour and without-undue-delay clocks for personal data breaches; and **Article 50** transparency duties apply to AI interaction and synthetic content.

### Preparedness

An AI incident response plan should be standalone or, preferably, integrated with the organization's IT, cybersecurity and privacy plans. Playbooks, simulation exercises and employee training are what make the plan real.
t_incident.exam:
Three questions dominate. Is this an incident or an issue? The answer turns on severity and context, not on the type of event. What is the correct first action? Preserve evidence and the audit trail, then triage, and do not retrain or disable logging. Who must be notified, and when? EU AI Act Article 73 serious incident reporting for high-risk providers, GDPR Articles 33 and 34 for personal data breaches, and the AI Act's transparency duties for user-facing systems.

The trap is the answer that sounds decisive but destroys evidence: retraining the model, deleting the logs, or rolling back before the state has been captured. The second trap is treating every incident as a bug when the cause is a misaligned objective. The third is forgetting that a near miss and a systemic-risk indicator both count: repeated human overrides or a spike in edge-case failures are tripwires, not noise.

t_records.overview: Business records are the evidence layer of AI governance: incident and issue logs, the risk register, post-market monitoring plans, decisions and approvals, model versions and data lineage. They are what makes accountability demonstrable rather than asserted, and they are the first thing an auditor or regulator asks for. Localization policy sits in the same topic because the decision to restrict a system to a region is itself a documented control with records attached.
t_records.deep_dive:
### What has to be written down

Record keeping in this domain covers four families:

- **Incidents and issues.** Incident records document events that deviate from intended behaviour, with the date and time of detection, the detection source, the system or model affected, the observed behaviour and consequences, the severity classification, the immediate response and who took it, the root cause, the mitigation and its verification, and the resolution date. Issue records track less severe items through intake, categorization, assignment, escalation, resolution and closure.
- **Risks.** The risk register, with the system or application, description, associated use cases, likelihood and impact scores, treatment decision and decision-maker, mitigation strategy, residual risk, owner and review schedule.
- **Post-market monitoring plans.** The documented, forward-looking plan established before release: what real-world data is collected, how it is reviewed, by whom, and what thresholds trigger action.
- **Lifecycle artifacts.** Design documents, training data provenance and lineage, test plans and results, model versions, configuration records, human intervention logs, and the approvals that authorized each stage.

### The legal hooks

The obligations differ by jurisdiction and by role, and the exam tests the specific ones. Under the **EU AI Act**, high-risk systems carry detailed technical documentation duties for providers (Article 11 and Annex IV), and deployers must keep the system's automatically generated **logs for at least six months** under **Article 26(6)** unless other law provides otherwise. Under the **GDPR**, Article 30 requires records of processing activities, and the accountability principle in Article 5(2) requires the controller to be able to demonstrate compliance, which in practice means logging for automated decisions. NIST AI RMF expects documentation at every stage for trustworthiness and auditability, and ISO/IEC 42001 requires logging, incident reporting and risk documentation inside the management system.

### Retention, immutability and disposal

Records belong in the organization's retention schedule, typically three to seven years depending on jurisdiction, with periods set by system type and risk level. Most records should be **immutable**, held in a tamper-evident format, access-controlled to authorized personnel, and disposed of at end of life in proportion to the sensitivity of what they contain. Append-only logs and cryptographic hashing are the common mechanisms, and their purpose is **nonrepudiation**: a record that cannot be denied or quietly altered.

Deletion is a trap in both directions. Retaining personal data longer than necessary breaches data minimisation; deleting incident records at shutdown destroys the evidence that affected individuals may contest a past decision and that a regulator may examine years later. The right answer is a documented decision, made with legal counsel, per record type.

### Localization policy

A **localization policy** restricts a system's operation to specific regions, jurisdictions or contexts, and is the regional counterpart to deactivation. The drivers are data sovereignty laws requiring training or inference inside national borders, regional ethical and societal norms affecting content filtering or recommendations, and regulatory constraints such as an EU AI Act prohibition or a high-risk classification in one market only. The delivery options are separate country-specific model instances, federated learning that keeps data resident while training is decentralized, or a modular architecture that enables regional features selectively. Localization is a documented control, so the policy states the trigger, the decision authority, the technical mechanism, and the records that prove which version ran where.

Expect items on retention periods, on which artifact satisfies which obligation, and on what a specific record must contain. Two numbers are worth knowing exactly: EU AI Act Article 26(6) requires deployers of high-risk systems to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, and GDPR Article 30 requires records of processing activities. The GDPR Article 33 breach clock is 72 hours.

The trap is the deletion instinct. A scenario about retiring a system will offer prompt deletion of all records as a data-minimisation win, and the correct answer is that model versions, decision logs and documentation are preserved per retention obligations, because affected individuals and regulators can reach back long after shutdown. The second trap is an audit question where the organization has records but they are mutable: records that can be edited fail the nonrepudiation test.

t_comms.overview: An external communication plan is the documented strategy for what the organization says about an AI system, to whom, and through whom: capabilities and limitations, incident notifications, regulatory reporting and user-facing transparency. The BOK treats it as a governance artifact with owners and approvals, not a marketing function, and the exam tests it mainly through disclosure triggers and the danger of overclaiming.
t_comms.deep_dive:
### The governance structure

Communications need planning, discipline and maturity rather than ad hoc statements. The plan names the roles (a public information officer or equivalent as the authorized voice, a social media lead, an AI communications lead who owns the AI-specific messaging, legal counsel reviewing for compliance, IP and liability, and product or engineering staff supplying technical explanation), the channels, and the approval rule: communication to any external party is formally approved by a designated leader. It integrates with enterprise risk management, data governance, privacy, incident response and regulatory reporting, so that a disclosure is one motion rather than several departments acting separately.

### What gets disclosed

Capability and limitation disclosure covers the purpose and use cases, limitations and known risks (accuracy boundaries, potential biases, data dependencies, reliability caveats), how and when human oversight is used, general descriptions of data sources and model behaviour, and how to raise an inquiry, appeal a decision or correct an error. It appears through product documentation, terms of use, privacy notices, model cards and plain-language explainers.

The recurring warning is **overclaiming**. Overstating what a system can do invites regulatory scrutiny, loses consumer trust and creates litigation exposure, which is why accuracy claims about AI capability get the same review as any other public claim.

### The legal obligations that actually bite

| Obligation | Source |
|---|---|
| Tell people they are interacting with an AI system, unless it is obvious | EU AI Act Article 50(1), applying from 2 August 2026 |
| Mark synthetic and deepfake content | EU AI Act Article 50 |
| Report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority | EU AI Act Article 73 |
| Notify a personal data breach to the supervisory authority within 72 hours | GDPR Article 33 |
| Communicate a high-risk breach to affected data subjects without undue delay | GDPR Article 34 |
| Public registration of high-risk systems | EU AI Act, with intended purpose, technical specifications, risk mitigation and post-market monitoring plan |

The practical preparation is pre-approved templates: press releases, FAQ answers, timeline graphics and plain-language explanations of model behaviour, kept ready so that a time-sensitive disclosure does not have to be drafted under pressure.

### Crisis communication

A crisis plan names the response team and the people authorized to speak, frames the message around transparency, responsibility and the action being taken, and pre-writes the statements and anticipated questions. The reason it belongs in the AI governance plan rather than the comms team's folder is that the AI-specific scenarios (a model producing infringing content, a discriminatory outcome at scale, a security compromise of an agent) are foreseeable, and the response is judged on whether the organization was prepared.

### Across the lifecycle

Communication is mapped to lifecycle stage: design and development (research publications, data use notices), validation and testing (accuracy disclosures, bias audit results), deployment (purpose statement, user guidance, stakeholder briefings), operation (post-market updates, incident alerts, FAQs) and retirement (sunset notices, archival disclosures, user offboarding). Effectiveness is measured on clarity, reach, responsiveness and trust indicators, using surveys, sentiment analysis, inquiry volume and resolution time, with periodic communication audits to check clarity, consistency and legal adequacy.

The trap is a scenario where the organization wants to publicize a capability claim before validation, or to describe a model as more capable than the evidence supports. Overclaiming is the wrong answer even when it would help adoption. The second trap is treating retirement as needing no communication: sunset notices, archival disclosures and offboarding information are part of the plan.
